statements.text: AI is a transformative tool, and like other tools that can move society forward, but is also ripe for abuse. We see this abuse already happening. China's implementation of AI has allowed for mass surveillance of innocent Chinese citizens who have no chance at privacy.
statements.context: Senate hearing on AI and machine learning applications for the Department of Defense, where Senator Schmitt questions witnesses about U.S. tech companies' AI research in China.

statements.text: The scary thing about AI is that AI only strengthens a communist regime's ability to control the flow of information. All of these assumptions that were made for a very long-time sort of go out the window.
statements.context: Senate hearing on AI and machine learning applications for Department of Defense operations.

statements.text: I think there is a—there is a concern, at least that I have, that a regulatory scheme or we are doing something that sort of protects the big players, but ultimately leaves out the innovation, again that got us to this point now.
statements.context: Senate hearing on AI's potential to fuel economic growth and improve governance, during a Q&A exchange with expert witnesses.

statements.text: The worse thing we could do in this race towards AI is stifle innovation by unleashing the bureaucrats and putting crippling regulations onto innovators.
statements.context: Senator Schmitt delivers opening remarks at a Senate hearing on artificial intelligence and economic growth, framing U.S. AI leadership against Chinese and European competition.

statements.text: how would that concentration of power that could even be exacerbated than what we have right now under that kind of regime—how would that affect privacy, competition, consumer choice in the AI industry?
statements.context: Senator Schmitt poses a follow-up question during a Senate hearing on AI, privacy, and market concentration.

statements.text: While I believe targeted measures may be warranted where current gaps in law may exist it is critical that we are not over reactive.
statements.context: Senate hearing titled "The Need to Protect Americans' Privacy and the AI Accelerant," where Senator Schmitt delivers opening remarks and poses a question to a witness.

statements.text: Mr. Reed, given the rapid pace of AI innovation, especially among startups and individual developers, can you explain how such a regulation might disproportionately impact, if we were to follow this potentially where some people want to go, disproportionately impacts smaller entities that lack the resources of bigger tech companies?
statements.context: Senate hearing statement titled 'The Need to Protect Americans' Privacy and the AI Accelerant', where Senator Schmitt questions a witness about the regulatory burden on smaller AI developers.

statements.text: But my hope is that it is sort of a Sputnik moment for us, that our focus is less about controlling this, which some of the proposals we have seen in the last couple years are about controlling or locking in incumbents.
statements.context: Senator Schmitt speaking during the Senate Commerce Committee nomination hearing for Howard Lutnick as Secretary of Commerce.

statements.text: And I think when Europe is really messed up on AI as it has been overregulated and it is—they are sort of pushing a political bias, which has, I think, demolished Europe's chances at being a leader in this, which I guess that is good for us. [...] But how do we avoid that? How do we avoid woke AI? How do we avoid black George Washington? Like what do we do to make sure that this doesn't become the next frontier for this level of censorship, with quantum chips fueling it?
statements.context: Senate hearing on the nomination of Michael Kratsios for OSTP Director, with Senator Schmitt questioning the nominee about avoiding political bias and censorship in AI.

statements.text: What do you think the biggest challenge is right now for the United States to be the leader—and AI gets thrown around, you know, sort of broadly, but to be the leader in kind of innovation? And, you know, obviously DeepSeek is a wakeup call. I mean, there is no way they did it for $6 million. But the fact is, I think our assumptions about how far ahead we were, have been shattered to some degree, right. So this is a very serious race we have with China. What do you think our biggest obstacle is to continue to be the leader?
statements.context: Senate confirmation hearing for the OSTP Director nominee, where Senator Schmitt questions the nominee about US AI competitiveness.

statements.text: One of the concerns I think a lot of folks have is that what you do not want to have is AI manipulated in a way that affects people's right to express themselves or free speech, and that will be sort of on your plate, too.
statements.context: Senate confirmation hearing for Paul Dabbar as Deputy Secretary of Commerce.

statements.text: one of the concerns I have with AI, I suppose, is that if we end up with a place where it is somehow policing, quote/unquote, ``misinformation''
statements.context: Senate hearing titled "Winning the AI Race: Strengthening U.S. Capabilities in Computing and Innovation."

statements.text: Because right now the best estimates, I suppose, right, is that—I do not know, with China is 2 months to 6 months behind maybe on large language models. Hopefully, some of the advances we are seeing in the U.S. maybe there is a degree of separation. It is hard to know exactly, right, with DeepSeek. [...] But then you get down to the chips and that advantage is more like a couple of years probably, something like that. [...] So if that is where we are headed does that increase the U.S.' advantage, in your view, or does that sort of allow China to catch up quicker as we get more vertically integrated?
statements.context: Senate hearing titled 'Winning the AI Race: Strengthening U.S. Capabilities in Computing and Innovation'.

statements.text: What, I mean if anything, is your view or the Federal Government's view on whether it is disclosure requirements or audit standards or something, because we are headed down a road where—I mean we have seen this sort of dialog that led to a suicide also recently.
statements.context: Senate hearing titled "AI've Got a Plan: America's AI Action Plan," featuring a senator questioning a witness about LLM bias and potential regulatory remedies.

statements.text: The NIST, AI Risk Management Framework Guidance advises developers, this is a government agency, advises developers to mitigate risks related to quote, ``Harmful bias'' and content that may not, quote, ``distinguish fact from opinion or fiction''.
statements.context: Senate Judiciary Committee oversight hearing on government pressure on Big Tech content moderation, featuring witness questioning.
